L1: # `locale` — Internationalization services【0†¶】
L2: 
L3: Source code: 【1†Lib/locale.py†github.com】
L4: 
L5: * * *
L6: 
L7: The `locale` module opens access to the POSIX locale database and functionality. The POSIX locale mechanism allows programmers to deal with certain cultural issues in an application, without requiring the programmer to know all the specifics of each country where the software is executed.
L8: The `locale` module is implemented on top of the `_locale` module, which in turn uses an ANSI C locale implementation if available.
L9: 
L10: The `locale` module defines the following exception and functions:
L11: 
L12: exception locale.Error【2†¶】
L13: 
L14: 
L15: Exception raised when the locale passed to 【3†`setlocale()`】 is not recognized.
L16: 
L17: locale.setlocale(category, locale=None)【3†¶】
L18: If locale is given and not `None`, `setlocale()` modifies the locale setting for the category. The available categories are listed in the data description below. locale may be a 【4†string】, or a pair, language code and encoding. An empty string specifies the user’s default settings. If the modification of the locale fails, the exception 【2†`Error`】 is raised. If successful, the new locale setting is returned.
L19: If locale is a pair, it is converted to a locale name using the locale aliasing engine. The language code has the same format as a 【4†locale name】, but without encoding. The language code and encoding can be `None`.
L20: 
L21: If locale is omitted or `None`, the current setting for category is returned.
L22: Example:
L23: 
L24:     >>> import locale
L25:     >>> loc = locale.setlocale(locale.LC_ALL)  # get current locale
L26:     # use German locale; name and availability varies with platform
L27:     >>> locale.setlocale(locale.LC_ALL, 'de_DE.UTF-8')
L28:     >>> locale.strcoll('f\xe4 n', 'foo')  # compare a string containing an umlaut
L29:     >>> locale.setlocale(locale.LC_ALL, '')   # use user's preferred locale
L30:     >>> locale.setlocale(locale.LC_ALL, 'C')  # use default (C) locale
L31:     >>> locale.setlocale(locale.LC_ALL, loc)  # restore saved locale
L32: `setlocale()` is not thread-safe on most systems. Applications typically start with a call of:
L33: 
L34:     import locale
L35:     locale.setlocale(locale.LC_ALL, '')
L36: 
L37: 
L38: This sets the locale for all categories to the user’s default setting (typically specified in the `LANG` environment variable). If the locale is not changed thereafter, using multithreading should not cause problems.
L39: 
L40: Changed in version 3.15: Support language codes with `@`-modifiers.
L41: 
L42: locale.localeconv()【5†¶】
L43: Returns the database of the local conventions as a dictionary. This dictionary has the following strings as keys:
L44: Category  | Key  | Meaning
L45: --- | --- | ---
L46: 【6†`LC_NUMERIC`】  | `'decimal_point'`  | Decimal point character.
L47:  | `'grouping'`  | Sequence of numbers specifying which relative positions the `'thousands_sep'` is expected. If the sequence is terminated with 【7†`CHAR_MAX`】, no further grouping is performed. If the sequence terminates with a `0`, the last group size is repeatedly used.
L48:  | `'thousands_sep'`  | Character used between groups.
L49: 【8†`LC_MONETARY`】  | `'int_curr_symbol'`  | International currency symbol.
L50:  | `'currency_symbol'`  | Local currency symbol.
L51:  | `'p_cs_precedes/n_cs_precedes'`  | Whether the currency symbol precedes the value (for positive resp. negative values).
L52:  | `'p_sep_by_space/n_sep_by_space'`  | Whether the currency symbol is separated from the value by a space (for positive resp. negative values).
L53:  | `'mon_decimal_point'`  | Decimal point used for monetary values.
L54:  | `'frac_digits'`  | Number of fractional digits used in local formatting of monetary values.
L55:  | `'int_frac_digits'`  | Number of fractional digits used in international formatting of monetary values.
L56:  | `'mon_thousands_sep'`  | Group separator used for monetary values.
L57:  | `'mon_grouping'`  | Equivalent to `'grouping'`, used for monetary values.
L58:  | `'positive_sign'`  | Symbol used to annotate a positive monetary value.
L59:  | `'negative_sign'`  | Symbol used to annotate a negative monetary value.
L60:  | `'p_sign_posn/n_sign_posn'`  | The position of the sign (for positive resp. negative values), see below.
L61: All numeric values can be set to 【7†`CHAR_MAX`】 to indicate that there is no value specified in this locale.
L62: 
L63: The possible values for `'p_sign_posn'` and `'n_sign_posn'` are given below.
L64: Value  | Explanation
L65: --- | ---
L66: `0`  | Currency and value are surrounded by parentheses.
L67: `1`  | The sign should precede the value and currency symbol.
L68: `2`  | The sign should follow the value and currency symbol.
L69: `3`  | The sign should immediately precede the value.
L70: `4`  | The sign should immediately follow the value.
L71: `CHAR_MAX`  | Nothing is specified in this locale.
L72: The function temporarily sets the `LC_CTYPE` locale to the `LC_NUMERIC` locale or the `LC_MONETARY` locale if locales are different and numeric or monetary strings are non-ASCII. This temporary change affects other threads.
L73: 
L74: Changed in version 3.7: The function now temporarily sets the `LC_CTYPE` locale to the `LC_NUMERIC` locale in some cases.
L75: 
L76: locale.nl_langinfo(option)【9†¶】
L77: Return some locale-specific information as a string. This function is not available on all systems, and the set of possible options might also vary across platforms. The possible argument values are numbers, for which symbolic constants are available in the locale module.
L78: 
L79: The `nl_langinfo()` function accepts one of the following keys. Most descriptions are taken from the corresponding description in the GNU C library.
L80: 
L81: locale.CODESET【10†¶】
L82: Get a string with the name of the character encoding used in the selected locale.
L83: 
L84: locale.D_T_FMT【11†¶】
L85: 
L86: 
L87: Get a string that can be used as a format string for 【12†`time.strftime()`】 to represent date and time in a locale-specific way.
L88: 
L89: locale.D_FMT【13†¶】
L90: 
L91: 
L92: Get a string that can be used as a format string for 【12†`time.strftime()`】 to represent a date in a locale-specific way.
L93: 
L94: locale.T_FMT【14†¶】
L95: Get a string that can be used as a format string for 【12†`time.strftime()`】 to represent a time in a locale-specific way.
L96: 
L97: locale.T_FMT_AMPM【15†¶】
L98: 
L99: 
L100: Get a format string for 【12†`time.strftime()`】 to represent time in the am/pm format.
L101: 
L102: locale.DAY_1【16†¶】
L103: locale.DAY_2【17†¶】
L104: locale.DAY_3【18†¶】
L105: locale.DAY_4【19†¶】
L106: locale.DAY_5【20†¶】
L107: locale.DAY_6【21†¶】
L108: locale.DAY_7【22†¶】
L109: 
L110: 
L111: Get the name of the n-th day of the week.
L112: 
L113: Note
L114: This follows the US convention of 【16†`DAY_1`】 being Sunday, not the international convention (ISO 8601) that Monday is the first day of the week.
L115: 
L116: locale.ABDAY_1【23†¶】
L117: locale.ABDAY_2【24†¶】
L118: locale.ABDAY_3【25†¶】
L119: locale.ABDAY_4【26†¶】
L120: locale.ABDAY_5【27†¶】
L121: locale.ABDAY_6【28†¶】
L122: locale.ABDAY_7【29†¶】
L123: 
L124: 
L125: Get the abbreviated name of the n-th day of the week.
L126: locale.MON_1【30†¶】
L127: locale.MON_2【31†¶】
L128: locale.MON_3【32†¶】
L129: locale.MON_4【33†¶】
L130: locale.MON_5【34†¶】
L131: locale.MON_6【35†¶】
L132: locale.MON_7【36†¶】
L133: locale.MON_8【37†¶】
L134: locale.MON_9【38†¶】
L135: locale.MON_10【39†¶】
L136: locale.MON_11【40†¶】
L137: locale.MON_12【41†¶】
L138: 
L139: 
L140: Get the name of the n-th month.
L141: locale.ABMON_1【42†¶】
L142: locale.ABMON_2【43†¶】
L143: locale.ABMON_3【44†¶】
L144: locale.ABMON_4【45†¶】
L145: locale.ABMON_5【46†¶】
L146: locale.ABMON_6【47†¶】
L147: locale.ABMON_7【48†¶】
L148: locale.ABMON_8【49†¶】
L149: locale.ABMON_9【50†¶】
L150: locale.ABMON_10【51†¶】
L151: locale.ABMON_11【52†¶】
L152: locale.ABMON_12【53†¶】
L153: 
L154: 
L155: Get the abbreviated name of the n-th month.
L156: 
L157: locale.RADIXCHAR【54†¶】
L158: 
L159: 
L160: Get the radix character (decimal dot, decimal comma, etc.).
L161: 
L162: locale.THOUSEP【55†¶】
L163: 
L164: 
L165: Get the separator character for thousands (groups of three digits).
L166: locale.YESEXPR【56†¶】
L167: 
L168: 
L169: Get a regular expression that can be used with the regex function to recognize a positive response to a yes/no question.
L170: 
L171: locale.NOEXPR【57†¶】
L172: 
L173: 
L174: Get a regular expression that can be used with the `regex(3)` function to recognize a negative response to a yes/no question.
L175: 
L176: Note
L177: 
L178: The regular expressions for 【56†`YESEXPR`】 and 【57†`NOEXPR`】 use syntax suitable for the `regex` function from the C library, which might differ from the syntax used in 【58†`re`】.
L179: locale.CRNCYSTR【59†¶】
L180: 
L181: 
L182: Get the currency symbol, preceded by “-” if the symbol should appear before the value, “+” if the symbol should appear after the value, or “.” if the symbol should replace the radix character.
L183: 
L184: locale.ERA【60†¶】
L185: 
L186: 
L187: Get a string which describes how years are counted and displayed for each era in a locale.
L188: Most locales do not define this value. An example of a locale which does define this value is the Japanese one. In Japan, the traditional representation of dates includes the name of the era corresponding to the then-emperor’s reign.
L189: Normally it should not be necessary to use this value directly. Specifying the `E` modifier in their format strings causes the 【12†`time.strftime()`】 function to use this information. The format of the returned string is specified in The Open Group Base Specifications Issue 8, paragraph 【61†7.3.5.2 LC_TIME C-Language Access†pubs.opengroup.org】.
L190: 
L191: locale.ERA_D_T_FMT【62†¶】
L192: 
L193: 
L194: Get a format string for 【12†`time.strftime()`】 to represent date and time in a locale-specific era-based way.
L195: locale.ERA_D_FMT【63†¶】
L196: 
L197: 
L198: Get a format string for 【12†`time.strftime()`】 to represent a date in a locale-specific era-based way.
L199: 
L200: locale.ERA_T_FMT【64†¶】
L201: 
L202: 
L203: Get a format string for 【12†`time.strftime()`】 to represent a time in a locale-specific era-based way.
L204: 
L205: locale.ALT_DIGITS【65†¶】
L206: 
L207: 
L208: Get a string consisting of up to 100 semicolon-separated symbols used to represent the values 0 to 99 in a locale-specific way. In most locales this is an empty string.
L209: The function temporarily sets the `LC_CTYPE` locale to the locale of the category that determines the requested value (`LC_TIME`, `LC_NUMERIC`, `LC_MONETARY` or `LC_MESSAGES`) if locales are different and the resulting string is non-ASCII. This temporary change affects other threads.
L210: 
L211: Changed in version 3.14: The function now temporarily sets the `LC_CTYPE` locale in some cases.
L212: 
L213: locale.getdefaultlocale([envvars])【66†¶】
L214: Tries to determine the default locale settings and returns them as a tuple of the form `(language code, encoding)`.
L215: 
L216: According to POSIX, a program which has not called `setlocale(LC_ALL, '')` runs using the portable `'C'` locale. Calling `setlocale(LC_ALL, '')` lets it use the default locale as defined by the `LANG` variable. Since we do not want to interfere with the current locale setting we thus emulate the behavior in the way described above.
L217: To maintain compatibility with other platforms, not only the `LANG` variable is tested, but a list of variables given as envvars parameter. The first found to be defined will be used. envvars defaults to the search path used in GNU gettext; it must always contain the variable name `'LANG'`. The GNU gettext search path contains `'LC_ALL'`, `'LC_CTYPE'`, `'LANG'` and `'LANGUAGE'`, in that order.
L218: The language code has the same format as a 【4†locale name】, but without encoding and `@`-modifier. The language code and encoding may be `None` if their values cannot be determined. The “C” locale is represented as `(None, None)`.
L219: 
L220: locale.getlocale(category=LC_CTYPE)【67†¶】
L221: 
L222: 
L223: Returns the current setting for the given locale category as a tuple containing the language code and encoding. category may be one of the `LC_*` values except 【68†`LC_ALL`】. It defaults to 【69†`LC_CTYPE`】.
L224: The language code has the same format as a 【4†locale name】, but without encoding. The language code and encoding may be `None` if their values cannot be determined. The “C” locale is represented as `(None, None)`.
L225: 
L226: Changed in version 3.15: `@`-modifier are no longer silently removed, but included in the language code.
L227: 
L228: locale.getpreferredencoding(do_setlocale=True)【70†¶】
L229: Return the 【71†locale encoding】 used for text data, according to user preferences. User preferences are expressed differently on different systems, and might not be available programmatically on some systems, so this function only returns a guess.
L230: 
L231: On some systems, it is necessary to invoke 【3†`setlocale()`】 to obtain the user preferences, so this function is not thread-safe. If invoking setlocale is not necessary or desired, do_setlocale should be set to `False`.
L232: On Android or if the 【72†Python UTF-8 Mode】 is enabled, always return `'utf-8'`, the 【71†locale encoding】 and the do_setlocale argument are ignored.
L233: 
L234: The 【73†Python preinitialization】 configures the LC_CTYPE locale. See also the 【74†filesystem encoding and error handler】.
L235: 
L236: Changed in version 3.7: The function now always returns `"utf-8"` on Android or if the 【72†Python UTF-8 Mode】 is enabled.
L237: 
L238: locale.getencoding()【75†¶】
L239: 
L240: 
L241: Get the current 【71†locale encoding】:
L242:   * On Android and VxWorks, return `"utf-8"`.
L243: 
L244:   * On Unix, return the encoding of the current 【69†`LC_CTYPE`】 locale. Return `"utf-8"` if `nl_langinfo(CODESET)` returns an empty string: for example, if the current LC_CTYPE locale is not supported.
L245: 
L246:   * On Windows, return the ANSI code page.
L247: 
L248: The 【73†Python preinitialization】 configures the LC_CTYPE locale. See also the 【74†filesystem encoding and error handler】.
L249: This function is similar to 【70†`getpreferredencoding(False)`】 except this function ignores the 【72†Python UTF-8 Mode】.
L250: 
L251: Added in version 3.11.
L252: 
L253: locale.normalize(localename)【76†¶】
L254: 
L255: 
L256: Returns a normalized locale code for the given locale name. The returned locale code is formatted for use with 【3†`setlocale()`】. If normalization fails, the original name is returned unchanged.
L257: If the given encoding is not known, the function defaults to the default encoding for the locale code just like 【3†`setlocale()`】.
L258: 
L259: locale.strcoll(string1, string2)【77†¶】
L260: 
L261: 
L262: Compares two strings according to the current 【78†`LC_COLLATE`】 setting. As any other compare function, returns a negative, or a positive value, or `0`, depending on whether string1 collates before or after string2 or is equal to it.
L263: 
L264: locale.strxfrm(string)【79†¶】
L265: Transforms a string to one that can be used in locale-aware comparisons. For example, `strxfrm(s1) < strxfrm(s2)` is equivalent to `strcoll(s1, s2) < 0`. This function can be used when the same string is compared repeatedly, e.g. when collating a sequence of strings.
L266: 
L267: locale.format_string(format, val, grouping=False, monetary=False)【80†¶】
L268: Formats a number val according to the current 【6†`LC_NUMERIC`】 setting. The format follows the conventions of the `%` operator. For floating-point values, the decimal point is modified if appropriate. If grouping is `True`, also takes the grouping into account.
L269: 
L270: If monetary is true, the conversion uses monetary thousands separator and grouping strings.
L271: 
L272: Processes formatting specifiers as in `format % val`, but takes the current locale settings into account.
L273: Changed in version 3.7: The monetary keyword parameter was added.
L274: 
L275: locale.currency(val, symbol=True, grouping=False, international=False)【81†¶】
L276: 
L277: 
L278: Formats a number val according to the current 【8†`LC_MONETARY`】 settings.
L279: 
L280: The returned string includes the currency symbol if symbol is true, which is the default. If grouping is `True` (which is not the default), grouping is done with the value. If international is `True` (which is not the default), the international currency symbol is used.
L281: 
L282: Note
L283: This function will not work with the ‘C’ locale, so you have to set a locale via 【3†`setlocale()`】 first.
L284: 
L285: locale.str(float)【82†¶】
L286: 
L287: 
L288: Formats a floating-point number using the same format as the built-in function `str(float)`, but takes the decimal point into account.
L289: 
L290: locale.delocalize(string)【83†¶】
L291: 
L292: 
L293: Converts a string into a normalized number string, following the 【6†`LC_NUMERIC`】 settings.
L294: 
L295: Added in version 3.5.
L296: 
L297: locale.localize(string, grouping=False, monetary=False)【84†¶】
L298: Converts a normalized number string into a formatted string following the 【6†`LC_NUMERIC`】 settings.
L299: 
L300: Added in version 3.10.
L301: 
L302: locale.atof(string, func=float)【85†¶】
L303: 
L304: 
L305: Converts a string to a number, following the 【6†`LC_NUMERIC`】 settings, by calling func on the result of calling 【83†`delocalize()`】 on string.
L306: 
L307: locale.atoi(string)【86†¶】
L308: 
L309: 
L310: Converts a string to an integer, following the 【6†`LC_NUMERIC`】 conventions.
L311: 
L312: locale.LC_CTYPE【69†¶】
L313: Locale category for the character type functions. Most importantly, this category defines the text encoding, i.e. how bytes are interpreted as Unicode codepoints. See 【87†PEP 538†peps.python.org】 and 【88†PEP 540†peps.python.org】 for how this variable might be automatically coerced to `C.UTF-8` to avoid issues created by invalid settings in containers or incompatible settings passed over remote SSH connections.
L314: Python doesn’t internally use locale-dependent character transformation functions from `ctype.h`. Instead, `pyctype.h` provides locale-independent equivalents like 【89†`Py_TOLOWER`】.
L315: 
L316: locale.LC_COLLATE【78†¶】
L317: 
L318: 
L319: Locale category for sorting strings. The functions 【77†`strcoll()`】 and 【79†`strxfrm()`】 of the `locale` module are affected.
L320: 
L321: locale.LC_TIME【90†¶】
L322: 
L323: 
L324: Locale category for the formatting of time. The function 【12†`time.strftime()`】 follows these conventions.
L325: 
L326: locale.LC_MONETARY【8†¶】
L327: Locale category for formatting of monetary values. The available options are available from the 【5†`localeconv()`】 function.
L328: 
L329: locale.LC_MESSAGES【91†¶】
L330: 
L331: 
L332: Locale category for message display. Python currently does not support application specific locale-aware messages. Messages displayed by the operating system, like those returned by 【92†`os.strerror()`】 might be affected by this category.
L333: 
L334: This value may not be available on operating systems not conforming to the POSIX standard, most notably Windows.
L335: locale.LC_NUMERIC【6†¶】
L336: 
L337: 
L338: Locale category for formatting numbers. The functions 【80†`format_string()`】, 【86†`atoi()`】, 【85†`atof()`】 and 【82†`str()`】 of the `locale` module are affected by that category. All other numeric formatting operations are not affected.
L339: 
L340: locale.LC_ALL【68†¶】
L341: Combination of all locale settings. If this flag is used when the locale is changed, setting the locale for all categories is attempted. If that fails for any category, no category is changed at all. When the locale is retrieved using this flag, a string indicating the setting for all categories is returned. This string can be later used to restore the settings.
L342: 
L343: locale.CHAR_MAX【7†¶】
L344: 
L345: 
L346: This is a symbolic constant used for different values returned by 【5†`localeconv()`】.
L347: ## Background, details, hints, tips and caveats【93†¶】
L348: 
L349: The C standard defines the locale as a program-wide property that may be relatively expensive to change. On top of that, some implementations are broken in such a way that frequent locale changes may cause core dumps. This makes the locale somewhat painful to use correctly.
L350: Initially, when a program is started, the locale is the `C` locale, no matter what the user’s preferred locale is. There is one exception: the 【69†`LC_CTYPE`】 category is changed at startup to set the current locale encoding to the user’s preferred locale encoding. The program must explicitly say that it wants the user’s preferred locale settings for other categories by calling `setlocale(LC_ALL, '')`.
L351: It is generally a bad idea to call 【3†`setlocale()`】 in some library routine, since as a side effect it affects the entire program. Saving and restoring it is almost as bad: it is expensive and affects other threads that happen to run before the settings have been restored.
L352: If, when coding a module for general use, you need a locale independent version of an operation that is affected by the locale (such as certain formats used with 【12†`time.strftime()`】), you will have to find a way to do it without using the standard library routine. Even better is convincing yourself that using locale settings is okay. Only as a last resort should you document that your module is not compatible with non-`C` locale settings.
L353: The only way to perform numeric operations according to the locale is to use the special functions defined by this module: 【85†`atof()`】, 【86†`atoi()`】, 【80†`format_string()`】, 【82†`str()`】.
L354: There is no way to perform case conversions and character classifications according to the locale. For (Unicode) text strings these are done according to the character value only, while for byte strings, the conversions and classifications are done according to the ASCII value of the byte, and bytes whose high bit is set (i.e., non-ASCII bytes) are never converted or considered part of a character class such as letter or whitespace.
L355: ## Locale names【94†¶】
L356: 
L357: The format of the locale name is platform dependent, and the set of supported locales can depend on the system configuration.
L358: 
L359: On Posix platforms, it usually has the format 【95†[1]】:
L360: 
L361:       language ["_" territory] ["." charset] ["@" modifier]
L362: where language is a two- or three-letter language code from 【96†ISO 639†www.iso.org】, territory is a two-letter country or region code from 【97†ISO 3166†www.iso.org】, charset is a locale encoding, and modifier is a script name, a language subtag, a sort order identifier, or other locale modifier (for example, “latin”, “valencia”, “stroke” and “euro”).
L363: On Windows, several formats are supported. 【98†[2]】 【99†[3]】 A subset of 【100†IETF BCP 47†www.rfc-editor.org】 tags:
L364: 
L365:       language ["-" script] ["-" territory] ["." charset]
L366:       language ["-" script] "-" territory "-" modifier
L367: where language and territory have the same meaning as in Posix, script is a four-letter script code from 【101†ISO 15924†www.unicode.org】, and modifier is a language subtag, a sort order identifier or custom modifier (for example, “valencia”, “stroke” or “x-python”). Both hyphen (`'-'`) and underscore (`'_'`) separators are supported. Only UTF-8 encoding is allowed for BCP 47 tags.
L368: 
L369: Windows also supports locale names in the format:
L370: 
L371:       language ["_" territory] ["." charset]
L372: where language and territory are full names, such as “English” and “United States”, and charset is either a code page number (for example, “1252”) or UTF-8. Only the underscore separator is supported in this format.
L373:

L387: ## For extension writers and programs that embed Python【108†¶】
L388: 
L389: Extension modules should never call 【3†`setlocale()`】, except to find out what the current locale is. But since the return value can only be used portably to restore it, that is not very useful (except perhaps to find out whether or not the locale is `C`).
L390: When Python code uses the `locale` module to change the locale, this also affects the embedding application. If the embedding application doesn’t want this to happen, it should remove the `_locale` extension module (which does all the work) from the table of built-in modules in the `config.c` file, and make sure that the `_locale` module is not accessible as a shared library.

L409: The locale module exposes the C library’s gettext interface on systems that provide this interface. It consists of the functions 【110†`gettext()`】, 【111†`dgettext()`】, 【112†`dcgettext()`】, 【113†`textdomain()`】, 【114†`bindtextdomain()`】, and 【115†`bind_textdomain_codeset()`】. These are similar to the same functions in the 【116†`gettext`】 module, but use the C library’s binary format for message catalogs, and the C library’s search algorithms for locating message catalogs.
L410: Python applications should normally find no need to invoke these functions, and should use 【116†`gettext`】 instead. A known exception to this rule are applications that link with additional C libraries which internally invoke C functions `gettext` or `dcgettext`. For these applications, it may be necessary to bind the text domain, so that the libraries can properly locate their message catalogs.
